title: Kenyan Sweet Millet Porridge
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: National — present in virtually every Kenyan community
heritage.history: Sweet millet porridge (uji wa wimbi) is Kenya's most deeply rooted breakfast tradition. Finger millet has been cultivated in East Africa for over 5,000 years, and porridge made from it has been the morning meal of Kenyan communities across the highlands, valleys, and coasts for just as long. It is the breakfast of infants, athletes, elders, and everyone in between. No other food is as universally Kenyan as uji.
heritage.modernEvolution: Commercially milled wimbi flour has made uji faster and more consistent to prepare. Many Kenyan families still mill their own finger millet at local posho mills for the most flavourful result.

desc: Kenyan Sweet Millet Porridge — finger millet flour cooked into a smooth, nourishing porridge, sweetened with sugar or honey and finished with a splash of milk. The most beloved and universally consumed breakfast in Kenya — simple, nutritious, and deeply comforting.
longDesc: Uji wa wimbi is the breakfast that has sustained Kenyans from generation to generation. The dark, earthy finger millet flour produces a porridge that is simultaneously nutty, slightly tangy, and deeply satisfying. Sweetened with sugar or honey and thinned with milk to the perfect drinking or spooning consistency, it is equally at home in a village homestead and a Nairobi apartment.
ingredients: 2—3 tbsp sugar or honey — to taste
½ cup milk or plant-based milk — to finish

substitutions.alternative: Honey — added off the heat to preserve live enzymes

steps: Mix millet flour with 1 cup of cold water to a smooth, lump-free slurry.
Bring remaining 3 cups of water to a rolling boil.
Reduce heat to medium. Pour the flour slurry into the hot water in a slow, steady stream, stirring constantly.
Stir vigorously and continuously for 8—10 minutes until the porridge thickens and the raw flour taste cooks out.
Add salt and sugar. Stir to dissolve.
Remove from heat. Stir in milk to achieve desired consistency.
Pour into cups or bowls. Serve immediately.
chefTips: The cold water slurry is non-negotiable — adding dry flour directly to hot water creates irreversible lumps.
Stir constantly once the slurry is added — millet porridge sticks and burns very quickly.
The porridge should be pourable like a thick soup — it thickens further as it cools.
Add honey off the heat to preserve its natural enzymes and complex flavour.
commonMistakes: Not making a cold slurry first — lumpy porridge.
Stopping stirring — burns on the bottom.

faqs.a: Finger millet's colour comes from tannins and anthocyanins in the bran — the same compounds that make it nutritionally exceptional. The darker the flour, the less processed and more nutritious it is.

faqs.q: Can I make it thicker for a spoon?
faqs.a: Yes — use 3 cups of water instead of 4, or simmer for longer. The Kenyan tradition ranges from completely liquid (drunk from a cup) to thick enough to eat with a spoon.

cookingScience: Finger millet starch gelatinises at around 72°C, transforming the slurry from a suspension into a thick, cohesive gel. The tannins in finger millet slow starch digestion, explaining its lower glycaemic index compared to refined grain porridges.
sustainabilityTips: Finger millet is one of the most drought-resistant cereal crops in East Africa — a climate-resilient food choice.
Supports smallholder millet farmers across Central and Eastern Kenya.
storage: Best consumed fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days — reheat with water.
reheating: Warm gently on stovetop with a splash of water, stirring continuously.
healthBenefits: Finger millet has the highest calcium content of any cereal — exceptional for bone health.
Rich in iron — beneficial for anaemia prevention.
High in dietary fibre — supports digestive health.
Low glycaemic index — provides sustained energy without blood sugar spikes.
culturalNote: Uji wa wimbi is Kenya's most universal food — the common thread running through every community, region, and generation. It is the first solid food given to Kenyan infants, the breakfast of Kenyan Olympic athletes, and the daily sustenance of millions. No food is more fundamentally Kenyan.
regionalVariations: Thin uji — drunk from a cup, popular in Central Kenya.
Thick uji — eaten with a spoon.
Uji with mursik — the Kalenjin and Maasai version (see KEN182).
Uji with coconut milk — popular on the coast.
Sorghum uji — lighter, more common in Western Kenya.
